Mechanisms of Action
Formation of Taurine Chloramine (TauCl): At sites of inflammation in the RA joint, activated neutrophils produce hypochlorous acid (HOCl), a potent oxidant. Taurine, which is abundant in these cells, reacts with HOCl to form TauCl, a less toxic, stable, anti-inflammatory agent. This reaction detoxifies the highly reactive HOCl, protecting surrounding tissue from damage.
Inhibition of Pro-inflammatory Cytokines: TauCl suppresses the production of key pro-inflammatory cytokines (such as IL-6, IL-8, IL-1β, and TNF-α) which are secreted by various immune cells, including T-cells and fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS), thus reducing overall inflammation in the joint.
Modulation of Transcription Factors: TauCl reduces the activity of major pro-inflammatory transcription factors like nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) and activator protein 1 (AP-1), which are crucial for the expression of inflammatory genes in T-cells and other immune cells.
Promotion of Regulatory T Cells (Tregs): Research indicates that taurine treatment can increase the abundance and function of CD4+CD25+FoxP3+ regulatory T cells (Tregs). Tregs are a specialized subset of T-cells that help suppress the immune response and prevent autoimmunity. This is mediated, in part, by inducing the release of the anti-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-35 (IL-35).
Suppression of T-cell Proliferation: TauCl has been shown to directly inhibit the proliferation of lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell that includes T-cells) , further reducing the overall inflammatory burden.
Regulation of Autophagy and Senescence: Recent studies suggest taurine may also target pathways related to cellular aging and waste removal (autophagy), such as the FOXO3-Parkin signaling pathway, which is often down-regulated in RA. By upregulating FOXO3 expression, taurine helps manage cellular health and reduce inflammation.

Author: @ThePashoushka
Content:
Thank you for the incredible video (as always)! 

I'm curious about the evidence that shows that bodies who died at a much lower rate during the black plague had genes which increase the risk for crohn's disease. I understand this as meaning that this gene helped them survived infectious diseases back them, supposedly because their immune systems would have been firing up more than non-crohn disease risk gene carriers, thus helping them fight off the infection. 

However, to my understanding, auto-immune diseases (AID) don't consistently have increased markers of infection in their blood. And as you said in the video, because specific types of auto immune diseases target specific tissues, e.g., auto immune thyroiditis targets thyroid proteins, they don't necessarily trigger generalised inflammation in the body, which would be useful to fight infectious diseases. 
So the evidence presented would make sense for AID of multiple systems (different organs, across the body), and in this case crohn's, but wouldn't necessarily be true for more specific AID. 

I'm also wondering if there are more recent research that could shed light to this, for example by looking at recovery time from infectious diseases in ppl with and without auto immune disease, and then comparing between ppl with AIDs such as crohn's and lupus vs type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroiditis. 

What do you all think? 
I'm curious! And maybe I should know more about the immune system but it seemed interesting to raise as a question.

Autoimmune diseases occur when the immune system mistakenly attacks the body’s own healthy tissues, leading to serious conditions like Type 1 diabetes, lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, or multiple sclerosis.They are caused by a combination of genetic predisposition and random trigger events, such as infections or viruses with protein structures similar to the body’s own.
Although these genes once helped our ancestors survive deadly pandemics, today they act like a double-edged sword, turning the immune system into a relentless enemy.

Content: I got diagnosed with psoriatic arthritis sine psoriasis as a teenager after years of constant stress. The amount of times I've been told by doctors that my pain is all in my head, or that there's nothing they can do to help me is staggering. Although I've started to come to terms with my reality, there's a part of me that will always wonder what my life could've been like if I hadn't been forced to grow up so fast. Thank you for shedding light on autoimmune diseases- it makes us feel seen.🎀

Author: @GalenerGelsdoorin
Content:
I have severe ulcerative colitis. It was the worst case my specialist had ever seen and called it a textbook case "Because you would only see it this bad in a textbook, but this is real!". I got diagnosed with it at the start of 2019 but had been dealing with pain for a few weeks, close to a month. It was a busy time at work leading up to and past the Christmas period and working in hospitality, it's not easy. So I was dealing with some stomach pains and I was putting it down to exhaustion. I just got on with it and pushed through the pain. After Christmas it was getting somewhat worse but I did nothing about it because I still really believed it was because I was being so over worked and under lots of stress. I didn't have time to stop and think about my own health and couldn't really take time off from work to go see a doctor because I thought would be a waste of time. Nothing serious!

I was working New Years Eve and was in a lot of pain. Spent most of the time holding my stomach. I was bullied into working the night shift there to midnight and so I was in pain the whole time, trying my best to get through it. 1st of January was my mums birthday and I didn't want to be a burden to anyone and so didn't say anything about the pain I was in. It was getting worse and I didn't eat much because of the pain. That night I was up most of the night throwing up. At around 6-ish in the morning my mother had woken up and I had still been throwing up and she said "You're going to the hospital" I protested saying "No, I'm fine. I don't want to put anyone out." but she made me go. Sat waiting in the hospital for a while and they did an xray and some tests and were like "Yeah, there is something serious going on here" and I was starting to freak out. They put me on so many IV medications and some saline to keep my fluids up and they told me I was lucky I came in when I did. I had a toxic mega colon which was very large and pushing against my heart and lungs and was close to bursting. They said if I had of waited another day or two it would have most likely burst and I would be dead. I was rushed to one of the bigger hospitals and was in a critical condition for like a week. Not allowed to eat or drink anything to be ready to be rushed into surgery in the event my toxic mega colon burst. I deal with some pain still at times and I have to get injections every 2 weeks for the rest of my life to suppress my immune system to stop it eating away at my intestines. Content:
My mom was diagnosed with MS 5-6 years ago, but the signs had been ongoing for far longer than that, maybe 7-10 years. Thankfully, shortly after being diagnosed, she was offered to try a then-new drug called Kasempta. She was among the very first people to start taking it, and I'm happy to say that ever since she's been taking it monthly, the progression of her MS has been pretty much entirely halted, and she hasn't gotten worse since. In a way, my mom is a prime living example that we are getting significantly better and better at combating autoimmune diseases.

For further clarification, I'm not saying the damage already done has been reversed, that's not what the drug was designed to do, but simply that practically no further damage has been done since administering Kasempta, which is the best case scenario. I was playing for my high school football team as well as 2 ice hockey teams as a goalie (one high school and one private club) I was maxed out on time that i would go out of my way to just find time to do absolutely nothing, literally nothing but lay down i was so constantly tired.

I would also be the type to never get sick very often, and when i did get sick it would be like hospital worthy sickness and pain. My thought over these last ten years of having type 1 is that my trigger was probably just pushing my body harder than it could really handle responsibly. I remember i did some summer CrossFit race at a sports camp i volunteered at, I was so determined to make it a win that i ended up just laying on the floor and basically almost had heatstroke (I live in a desert, where it gets up to 110 regularly during mid summer).

So yeah, my lesson from this is to find balance for your body. Because it can only take so much of a beating until you just end up breaking something. For me it was my pancreas, for others it's their legs, arms, eyes, anything. When you start to have to rely on other tools and medications just to stay alive really puts some perspective on your life and others.

Stay balanced and live life.

Author: @AleixoAlonso
Content:
Autoimmune diseases suck. Honestly, all diseases suck. In 2022, right in the middle of university finals, I was diagnosed with Multiple Sclerosis. It all started when my vision began to deteriorate. I saw an eye doctor, who referred me to a neurologist. After an MRI, they sent me straight to the ER and started me on a high dose of cortisol.

Since then, I’ve been on medication. Weekly self-administered injections into my thigh. If you've ever felt awful after a flu or COVID shot, imagine going through that every single week. I've already been hospitalized twice since the diagnosis: once when the entire right side of my body went numb, and another time when I lost all temperature sensation on that side.

I changed my diet to mostly vegan, started exercising more. I wasn’t overweight or unhealthy before, but now I feel like I weigh as much as a sheet of paper. I battle daily fatigue, recurring vision issues, and a constant flip of the coin between being able to concentrate or feeling ashamed for not being productive.

And the hardest part? You can’t see it. If you looked at me, you’d just see a thin guy working on 3D models. You wouldn’t know that I have to be extremely careful with my health. You wouldn’t see the fact that I’ll never be able to work at 100% again.

I get weird looks when I wear a mask while shopping. My immunosuppressant meds leave me vulnerable. But somehow, I’m the one who gets judged for protecting myself. Meanwhile, people with the flu stroll into class, coughing unmasked in crowded stores. Those who aren’t at risk often don’t care about those who are. And somehow, I'm the one who has to feel guilty for being at risk *and* for trying to stay safe.

I’m still in uni, and I already dread the day I’ll have to explain to a future employer that I physically can’t work 40 hours a week. If it’s not the disease holding me back, it’s the meds. Explaining that to someone who can’t see what’s wrong is exhausting.

MS didn’t just bring fatigue, pain, and brain fog. It brought anxiety, stress, and paranoia too. They don't know where it comes from, they don't know how to cure it. The first thing my doctor said after the diagnosis was something along the lines of: "You're young. This sucks." I've now had it for three years. Yes, it sucks.

For anyone with relapsing-remitting MS, when I got diagnosed 3 years ago I got put on a treatment called Ofatumamab (Kesimpta is the brand name I think) which is a monthly self injection at home, and it's so far stopped progression in it's tracks. Content: I have to disagree mostly with this video.  I personally have an auto immune disease that is systemic and was basically explained what I have in this video, from my nerves, to my joints, to my thyroid, to low energy, to muscle aches, I have all these symptoms.  I always believed it to be something, Lyme disease, or a virus… it took me over 10 years to figure out that what I found out is my case is actually chronic viruses like Epstein Barr viruses, human herpes virus 6, and even chicken pox.  Particularly these herpes viruses that never truly go away.  They can all reactivate and they can potentially stack on top of each other making it worse.  If they reactivate by a “trigger” they infect more cells, and more cells get infected.  Some of these herpes viruses infect immune cells that become chronically infected but don’t die and can’t be killed, they spill virus everywhere in the body into the tissues and then the immune system attacks the tissues where the virus spread.   The virus replicates via bad unhealthy foods, lack of sleep, and poor diet and certainly certain anti-viral herbs and medicines can control the illness.  This is what I believe happened and it makes more sense than the body just attacking itself.

Author: @ryanpotter128
Content:
I'm a bioinformatics researcher that works with autoimmunity; just wanted to say that I think this is an interesting twist on the hygiene hypothesis, and while that particular hypothesis has had quite a lot of evidence against it, I really like that this version reframes it that it isn't because we don't have diseases (or worms, I think was the original suggestion that gets referred back to) in our environment that the autoimmune system is overactive leading to allergies and autoimmune dysfunction, but rather that these same genes are related to things that let us survive specific events along the evolutionary path. 
I recommend also maybe a future video on the theory of protective autoimmunity, which has a growing amount of support for it. The simplified idea there being that the self-recognizing T and B cells are not perfectly deleted by the "murder university", but rather that some are "expected" to get through as a part of healthy function, perhaps in response to protein misfolds being presented by MHC-2 receptors.
I personally think failures in this proposed regulatory system may be responsible for the pathogenesis of certain conditions, I'd be interested to hear your take on it.

I became a stubborn patient and stopped taking all my meds because I wanted to be young and live my life. Fast forward to today I have bone erosions in my hands and feet and permanent damage in my right hand. I also would constantly get colds and flus that would take me out weeks at a time. It’s been hard having the body of an 80 year old when all you want to do is open water bottles by yourself and not be stiff first thing in the morning. It’s felt like a constant battle of me vs me but I’m getting better. I’ve changed my diet to lower my inflammation and I’m back on the meds. I figured side effects are better than being permanently disabled. To anyone struggling with this shit - I feel you. You are not alone, I know it’s not fair. Autoimmune diseases are often invisible so fk people who don’t get why you’re always sick or why you were limping yesterday but are fine today. Pat yourself on the back for everyday you get out of bed. You are amazing. May you find peace and ease in life. Sending lots of love from a girl with creaky joints 🇨🇦🙏🏽❤️

Author: @KnowledgeSmartExplained1
Content:
Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disease that affects the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord). The body's immune system mistakenly attacks myelin, the protective covering of nerve fibers, causing damage and disrupting nerve signals.
Summary:
Autoimmune disease: The immune system mistakenly attacks the body (myelin).
Central nervous system affected: The brain and spinal cord are damaged.
Demyelination: The protective covering of nerves is destroyed.
Disruption of nerve signals: Leads to a variety of symptoms.
No cure: The goal of treatment is to control symptoms and slow progression.
Causes:
The exact cause of MS is unknown, but it may involve genetic and environmental factors.
Symptoms:
MS can cause a variety of symptoms, including:
Fatigue
Numbness, tingling
Vision problems (double vision, blurred vision)
Muscle weakness, difficulty moving
Bladder and bowel dysfunction
Memory and cognitive problems
Pain
Difficulty with balance and coordination
Progression:
MS can progress in a variety of ways, but it often includes periods of relapse and remission, or a gradual progression over time.
Treatment:
Currently, there is no cure for MS, but there are treatments that can help control symptoms, slow the progression of the disease, and improve quality of life. Treatments may include medications, physical therapy, and other supportive therapies

Author: @BlackLionRampant
Content:
In Aug 2020, my grandmother developed ATP (autoimmune thrombocytopenic purpura), where your immune system targets your platelets. She had strange symptoms such as bloodshot eyes and bleeding from her gums, which she first thought came from her hitting herself in her sleep. But then she started developing bruises everywhere. We rushed her to the hospital and they found she had a platelet count of 1 (lowest normal value is 150). The doctors were cautious to take her case as they thought it might be an as yet unknown symptom of COVID (early on we knew very little about it). A hematologist diagnosed her eventually, and we were able to bring her illness under control. She never had a relapse after that frightful episode. 
The hematologist said it was a good thing it was ATP, as it was the least dangerous of those related illnesses. Worst case scenario was lupus, which would be very difficult to manage in a 90+ year old patient.

Author: @ivancoon
Content:
T1D in my mid-30s: My unlucky chain of events:

- 2020: I suddenly experienced a sharp, stabbing pain in my chest that made it hard to breathe. It lasted for one night, but by the next morning I felt fine.
I went to my primary care doctor. Blood tests came back normal, and I was referred to a pulmonologist. After spirometry and other respiratory tests, all of which were normal, I was told, "It was probably a strained muscle from your workouts."
- 2021: The same pain returned. I went back to the doctor. Again, nothing was found.
- 2022: It happened again... but this time it was much worse. I could barely breathe and felt like I was dying. I was rushed to the ER.
First, they ruled out heart issues. Next, they considered my appendix or gallbladder, since problems there can also cause intense pain.
It turned out to be gallstones... Got stuck, causing inflammation, which led to pancreatitis. They immediately started medication to reduce the inflammation and removed my gallbladder a few days later.
- 2023: One hot night, I drank ~4l of water within ~2h and was going to the bathroom between drinks, the thirst was insane. Something ain't right, so the next morning I tested my blood glucose before breakfast: 11 mmol/L (200 mg/dL). My HbA1c was slightly lower (10 mmol/L), but still well above normal.
That’s when I was diagnosed with Type 1 Diabetes (ICA & GAD antibodies present).

Looking back:
Through my own neglect: like not getting annual checkups with imaging that could’ve detected the gallstones, and a primary care doctor who missed the signs, a seemingly minor issue (gallstones) spiraled into a life-changing autoimmune disease (T1D).
So:
1) Find a good primary care doctor. Someone who listens, asks the right questions, and doesn’t brush things off.
2) Do the annual checkups, and make sure they’re thorough.

Author: @michaelmachiavelli
Content:
In 2014 I was hit by a drunk driver. After 2 years of surgeries to fix my body, I had 1 final surgery to swap out plates in my arm, because I broke my arm in a fall.
After the surgery in 2016 it started out slow, aches and pains. Then I suddenly started getting sick from eating gluten, I would throw up within hours of eating or drinking anything like beer or bread. I would find out later that my immune system was killing the good bacteria in my gut biome. 
Then after about a year, it took a turn for the worst. 
My father passed away and in the summer of 2017, I went to spread his ashes, we decided to drive the 14 hours to the beach resort. During our time there I got weaker and was getting sick frequently, to the point where I was throwing up almost after every meal. But it got so MUCH worse during the drive back, by the time I got out of the car, I could barely walk. My body was on fire, and I could barely move from fatigue. After a week, I went to the doctor, after an attempted procedure, I got so sick I ended up in the hospital, I was in-and-out for weeks and the doctors couldn't figure it out. 
Then one day when walking into my bedroom I accidentally banged my arm, no big deal, happens to everyone, happens all the time. But as the day went on a strange bruise developed. When I woke up the next day I had a hematoma the size of a golf ball. One doctor figured out that I was suffering from an autoimmune disorder. From that point forward everything changed.
I have spent the last 7 years in and out of hospitals, getting more and more medical treatments, with harsher and harsher side effects. I'm currently on IVIG and Inflixamab infusions multiple times a month. I take 11 daily meds and 1 weekly high dose methotrexate shot. 
All of these treatments and the doctors STILL don't know what autoimmune disease I have, but we manage the pain and the symptoms and side effects as best we can.
My life has completely shut down, I have to live like everyone did during the pandemic, I don't leave the house except for doctors appointments and infusions. When I leave I have to wear a mask and constantly use hand sanitizer. It's like the whole world moved on without me and I got stuck in 2020.
To be honest, I don't know why I wrote this, maybe it was to give an example, maybe just to tell my story, maybe I just needed to scream into the void. 
But to anyone who has to go through something like this, just know you're not alone, and as long as you breathe, there's a chance for a better day.

Author: @coolcat8b
Content:
I have RA since 2009.  I believe it was triggered by an brutal accident to my hand, where my index finger was flipped backward violently (but did not break).  Soon after, I developed a fever, and started hurting all over my joints (feet, knees, and hands especially).  I asked the doctors to confirm my suspicion, but they never did.  They kept saying no one can tell what triggers RA.  Well, what you said confirms my suspicion.

I remained an invalid for 2,5 years, was heavily medicated (with a lot of bad side effects).  I could not work, could barely dress myself with elastic pants!  Everything hurt: walking, holding anything, sleeping was hard because my hands hurt so much, and the sheets hurt my feet.

Then one day I decided I'd had enough of the pills and injections that did nothing, and I stopped everything.  A couple of months after that, I started to feel better, the side effects subsided.  I've been free of the fever and pain ever since (beginning of 2012).  I walk normally and can do most things like before.  The damage to my joints is permanent, but is not getting worse.  I have no idea what made it stop, but I'm glad it did before too much damage was done.  I still have mobility and independence, and no more pills / injections!

For all you RA sufferers out there, there's hope. 🥰

Author: @astriferoussprite
Content:
Treatments for autoimmune diseases can be real wild, too. I have Crohn's, and the thing keeping me in remission are biologic drugs. They're basically targeted antibodies for your own immune system—using its weapons against itself! Mine is an anti-TNF agent that prevents my immune cells from communicating as much with TNF-alpha, and while this means I'm at a slightly higher risk for infectious disease and really rare cancers, in practice it just means more colds and yearly TB tests.
Biologics were only discovered in the past few decades, and it's amazing how quickly they can turn Crohn's from "consistently in pain and exhausted and unable to digest anything" to "normal but ease up on the caffeine and alcohol." Medicine is consistently making new and exciting breakthroughs, and god willing, we'll start having permanent cures within our lifetimes.

Author: @3dosean541
Content:
Someone with Crohn's disease here, and I'd just like to clarify that Crohn's is not considered by everyone to be an autoimmune disease. From what I understand from  my doctor who studies IBD and Crohn's, Crohn's disease is more of a hyperactive and aggressive immune response, that induces your typical gastrointestinal immune response but way too often, early, and severely. The way they've described it is that the immune system for your GI tract is essentially hypersensitive, and will fire off a response at bad bacteria that comes in from what you eat, or irritation from hard shells and fibers way before it's actually harmful. This results in high levels of inflammation, tiredness, ulcers, etc., from the overzealous immune system. Many people with Crohn's also have trigger foods that cause a fairly immediate reaction as well, i.e. for me sweet potatoes, lemon juice, or seaweed create a near immediate and severe response while for some reason normal potatoes don't, Crohn's is weird.
The reason this is not considered the same as an autoimmune disease is because Crohn's targets unhealthy bacteria and irritable substances, rather than your own cells, while autoimmune disease is characterized by an immune response against your own cells. While the symptoms are similar, this is just because your cells get caught in the crossfire of excessive immune system activity, instead of being the direct targets of your immune system.

Content:
It is also possible to get overactive immune responses. In my case, a misidentification of my bacterial flora is causing an endless form of pseudomembranous colitis. The only reason I'm alive is due to an anti-mitotic drug designed for rheumatoid arthritis blocking the overall production of my neutrophils which were massacering my intestines for years.

For those who want to know: pseudomembranous colitis is basically a response which causes your immune system to mimic a C. Difficile infection response without you actually having the pathogen. For anybody who has seen what a C. Diff infection can do to someone, you can imagine what 13 plus years of that with 5 of them being crisis years did to me.

Author: @reverse_engineered
Content: The most important thing to remember about evolution: it's not about survival of the fittest, it's about being capable of maintaining your genes in the gene pool. If you have kids and they survive to have kids, your genes are passed on. If those genes happen to make you somehow superior at being able to do so, they may become more prolific in the population over time, but there are a lot of factors outside of genes that affect popularity. The only particularly bad mutations are the ones that prevent your genes from being propagated, such as infertility, early death, or particularly unattractive traits. Especially in our modern world where competition is less about inheritance of genes and more about inheritance of circumstances, a lot of harmful genetic mutations can continue to propagate through the generations. Some common examples: imperfect eyesight, asthma, and allergies.

Author: @Kefroth1
Content:
I think one of the biggest issues with having an autoimmune disease (at least in the US) is health care. I have Crohn's disease and it is managed through biologics like Humira and Remicade. Any sort of risk factors aside, there is a big issue with these biologics; you cannot stop taking them or your body may start to develop antibodies that will prevent the drug from working in the future. Thing is, these medicines are _extremely_ expensive. For example, Humira requires a two shots a month each costing around 2000 bucks. Now, insurance generally brings this cost down to nearly nothing for the patient but here is where it gets tricky. What if your health insurance is given to you by your employer and you are laid off? What happens if you want to try to change careers into a better paying job? Hopefully you can afford continued coverage through COBRA or something but the reality is, you might end up in a world of hurt that permanently breaks your ability to get treatment from the drug you were using. As a fun bonus, many autoimmune diseases flare up when you are under stress meaning that your anxieties about health coverage are actively working against your health!

As an aside, if you have an auto-immune disease, do some research on helminthic therapy. It may not be for you, but you should at least know it exists.

Author: @theonewholost1859
Content:
Hey! Great video, and I was honestly waiting for it for a while with how you've made previous immune system vids.

I have Transverse Myelitis (TM) which is an autoimmune disorder where your spine is the target, and my onset was when I was 13 a decade ago and had me going from completely normal to paralyzed from the neck down in 5 hours and dang near died, as it attacked from my C2 to my T1 vertebrae. Sadly, the conclusion was made that, like you said, I'm just VERY unlucky, as my specific case is 'idiopathic', which is doctor speak for 'we have no idea what triggered this', AKA no known cause. It's... crappy, and it is sad that there isn't really a solution to this, just pain. Still recovering to this day, and while I'm better off than before, I still need extreme assistance and am bound to a power wheelchair.

Also, I have psoriasis, which is another autoimmune disorder but extremely less harmful and targets the skin, and my father has ITP, which is an autoimmune disorder that attacks your platelets, which is definitely on the deadly end. Both of our events are long past, with his being when I was 7, but we're both considered in 'remission', because every day we wake up, we're rolling D20s on whether that day will be the day we relapse, and for both of us... well to say the least, we won't live a second go 'round.

But nonetheless, thank you so much for the video, it's always great to learn more!

And yes, both I and my father were tested to see if there were common genetic markers between us and other autoimmune cases, and nothing was found.

Another evolutionary reason for an aggressive immune system is fighting cancer (which is literally made of your own cells, just turned bad).

Too overzelous and it might start to kill healthy cells.

With aging and accumulated DNA damage, keeping this balance becomes harder and harder until eventually we end up falling to one side: Cancer (or some external infections) or auto-immune diseases

Author: @zakarm1
Content:
Got an aggressive but pretty standard bout of gut infection. A couple of weeks into antibiotics and I was back to normal. But the doctor asked me if I was an alcoholic. I dont drink at all. But all the blood test markers suggest alchoholism and borderline liver failure. a few scans later (CT, ultrasoud), My liver looks absolutley fine. 

Off to a specialist I go - pretty quickly diagnosed with IgG4-related cholangiopathy. No symptoms. only blood markers which show liver damage and insane T cell count and immuniglobin levels. something somewhere along the way caused my immune system to decide my billary system was the enemy. I take the suggested treatment of a steroid infusion in the oncology ward each week for a month. . . im one of the ones it doesnt work for. my only other options are related to chemo. 

I decide (being in my mid 30s) to just roll with it and see if it gets worse. Now about to turn 40, my markers are high but stable. Fatigue is very high much of the time (could be age or lifestyle) and im steadily drifting towards pernicious anemia (high and higher doses of b12 oral suplements needed to keep b12 high). Is that caused by auto-immune, not likely, but you always question it.  its strange knowing there is something wrong but you only know about it from medical tests. You dont know if you should lean into it and go full chemotherapy just incase or if the side effects of that process are worse than what you have. 

You start to get some of lifes free DLC and question if its related to age or ailment. . . funny old thing autoimmune diseases. Will it kill me? will it turn into the big "C". 'll check back in a few years . . . or not!

Author: @DatDudeAlek
Content:
I really enjoyed this video and its presentation of autoimmune diseases. However, there's two sides, I wish it had touched more upon: Living with the disease, and the long medical journey leading to the diagnosis. 

I am one of those very unlucky few, who has an extremely rare auto immune disease. It took doctors years to figure out, what was wrong. An awful long time. I lost weight and muscle mass, and doctors managed to come up with very different reasons, which didn't fit the bill. In the end, I was often "too young" or "too healthy otherwise", and so it took almost 8 years, before I had a diagnosis and medicine. 
Secondly, I now live with this disease, which affects many parts of my life, yet it is not visible to the naked eye, like fx. a broken arm. It affects me differently from day to day, yet people can't easily see this, and this leads to some unfortunate situations, where friends and family do not understand, that I am in pain, feeling unwell, extremely tired, etc... 

So thank you for the video, I hope you will continue this with more focus on living with autoimmune disease next, to inform more about the ones of us, who lives with a war inside every day.

Content:
I have been diagnosed with crohn's disease  around 3 years ago and it wasnt i had to follow a strict diet for around 9 months or a year i dont remember exactly before i was diagnosed with crohn's i had the following symptoms: every time i had lunch breakfast or dinner or anything even a freaking water i needes to run to the bathroom because if i didnt i would have pooped my pants but not the 'ohh i sense something coming i need to go toilet' no no no no no its the 'ohh my god just kill me' like when you jump off a cliff into the ocean and land on your stomach and we go to Budapest and they tested me for everything in the allergy section but: dairy: negative
Gluten: negative
Shrimp: negative
Anything else: negative
And they tested a sample of my poop and they called my parent to go to the: Heim Pál gyermekkórház tomorrow and they did an endoscopy and they started my diet but now every 8 weeks i need to go back for my control examination 
The control examination goes like this:i lay in there, they measure my height and weight and my pulse and then they make a blood pull then i get steroids not that kind i think that you use to buff up and then i get some 'só oldat' as they say, the it translates to salt solution i wait for it to drip down and before and during this procedure i cant eat and drink then i get my biological DMARDs i wait for it to drip down then i go home and this repeats. So yeah its hard and confusing and it sucks but i accepted it and live with it if i meet somebody new they cant tell i have crohn's disease.  Thank you kurzgesagt for making a video on autoimmune diseases. Post note i have to take every day D-vitamins and 1000mgs calcium and 100mg imuran.
